text: You have a grid of oranges. Zero is an empty cell, one is a fresh orange, and two is a rotten one. Every minute, any fresh orange next to a rotten one — up, down, left, or right — rots too. Return the number of minutes until no fresh orange is left, or negative one if that's impossible.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — all rotten oranges spread at the same time each minute, and a fresh orange that's walled off from every rotten one makes the answer negative one. Is that right?

Okay. Spreading outward at the same time and counting the minutes is a multi-source BFS. I seed all rotten oranges into the queue, then expand level by level — each level is one minute. I also keep a fresh counter, so I know when everything has rotted, and can return negative one if some fresh orange is never reached. Let me run through the example: two, one, one; one, one, zero; zero, one, one. It starts with six fresh oranges, and four minutes later all of them are rotten, so the answer is four. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to BFS from every fresh orange to its nearest rotten one and take the max — that's the square of m times n. This problem reminds me of multi-source BFS: every rotten orange is a starting point and they all spread in parallel, so seeding them together gives each cell its distance to the nearest rotten one in a single pass. The twist here is that I want the number of levels, so I process the queue one level at a time.

Here's the plan. One: push every rotten orange into the queue and count the fresh ones; if there are none, return zero. Two: while the queue isn't empty, snapshot its size and process exactly that many cells, rotting their fresh neighbors, then add one minute. Three: if fresh hits zero, return the minute; if the queue drains first, return negative one. One thing worth flagging — that size snapshot is the whole trick. The queue holds this minute's oranges and the ones they just infected, so without it, two minutes blend together and the count comes out wrong. There's a trade-off here. The fresh counter isn't optional — it's how I detect the walled-off case. And I write the rot back into the grid, so I don't need a visited array. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One scan seeds every rotten orange and counts the fresh ones, with an early return of zero. Then the BFS loop: snapshot the size, pop exactly that many, and rot only neighbors that are in bounds and still fresh — writing a two into the grid so nothing rots twice. If the queue empties, I return negative one. One thing worth flagging — return time plus one, not time. Time counts the minutes fully elapsed; the neighbor I'm rotting right now rots in the next minute, so when the last fresh one goes, the answer is time plus one.

Let's dry-run the code with the example. The rotten orange at zero, zero seeds the queue, with six fresh. The waves rot two, two, one, and then one orange. The decision happens in the last wave: the orange at two, two rots while time is still three, so fresh hits zero and I return three plus one — four. The empty cell at two, zero blocks one path, but everything else is reachable. That matches. Corner cases: no fresh oranges at the start returns zero from the guard. Fresh oranges but no rotten one means an empty queue, so negative one. And a fresh orange boxed in by empties leaves fresh above zero when the queue drains, so negative one.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is O of m times n — each cell enters and leaves the queue at most once. The space complexity is O of m times n for the queue. In the worst-case scenario, a grid that's almost all rotten puts nearly every cell in the queue at the start. Oh, one more thing — the level split is only there because I return a number of levels. If I only needed each cell's distance to the nearest source, I could write that into the cell and skip the counter; here, the size snapshot is essential.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You seeded all rotten oranges for a simultaneous spread, not just one. You snapshotted the queue size so each wave maps to exactly one minute, and explained the time plus one. And you used the fresh counter to detect the unreachable negative one case. Good work.
